title: Who gets to live in town housing — and on what terms?
body:
The Telluride Housing Authority Subcommittee is moving to hire outside consultants to do a comprehensive review of the town's employee rental housing policies. That means the rules governing who qualifies, for how long, and under what conditions could be on the table.

Some residents will say it's overdue — that the current policies have gaps or inequities worth fixing. Others may worry that a consultant-driven review opens the door to tightening eligibility or changing terms that working locals depend on right now.

What do you think this review should actually be for?

title: Gas-powered leaf blowers — Telluride's next ban?
body:
The Ecology Commission is looking at a proposal to prohibit combustion-powered lawn care equipment in Telluride, possibly including a phase-out ordinance aimed at commercial operators. Supporters would say cleaner air and quieter streets are worth it. Opponents — especially commercial landscapers — might argue the costs and logistics of switching equipment fall hardest on small operators who work here for a living. Nothing is decided yet; this is still at the discussion stage.

So where do you land: is a ban on gas-powered lawn equipment a reasonable step, or too much of a burden on the people doing the work?

title: The eligibility policy the school board just took up
body: The Telluride Board of Education took a first reading of Policy JJJ — a revised extracurricular eligibility policy that incorporates Colorado's statutory definitions of male and female for athletic team participation. It also updates rules for homeschooled, charter, and nonpublic-school students joining district activities. Some will say aligning with state statute is the right call — consistent, legally grounded, end of story. Others will say a policy built around those definitions excludes kids who belong on the field. The board hasn't voted yet. So where do you come down?
choices: The statute sets the right standard

title: A housing action plan — from the county this time
body:
The Board of County Commissioners has a housing action plan on its work session agenda, alongside a hazard mitigation plan update and some routine procurement items. Nothing's been voted on yet — this is still a work session.

Here's where people tend to split. Some residents think the county stepping up on housing is overdue and welcome another hand on the problem. Others wonder whether another plan — on top of what the town is already doing — is duplication, or whether county-level action looks meaningfully different from what's come before.

What do you think: does a county housing action plan move the needle, or is it more of the same?

title: A banner for the seniors — worth a policy change?
body:
The Parks & Recreation Commission is looking at adding a new category to the Town Park Pavilion Banner Policy: banners honoring Telluride high school senior athletes in winter sports organizations under contract with the town. Display would run from the first day back after holiday break through the end of ice rink season, with a $10 installation fee per banner.

Some will see it as a small, well-deserved nod to local kids. Others may wonder whether adding a new policy category for one group opens the door to more carve-outs down the line. Where do you draw the line on who gets recognized in public space?

title: The levy vote is set — but the ballot results came first
body:
The school board is debriefing November ballot results — including Ballot Measure 5A, the MLO — before a December 14 special meeting to approve the mill levy. So voters already weighed in, and now the board acts on what that means for school funding going forward. Some residents will say the process is working as it should: voters decide, the board follows through. Others will wonder whether a December special meeting, after the fact, leaves much room for the community to shape what comes next. Either way, the numbers from November set the table.

Does the sequence — ballot first, levy vote after — give you confidence in how school funding decisions get made up here, or does it leave you wanting more input along the way?

title: Pause the open space fund — again?
body:
Council is voting on second reading of an ordinance that would suspend the 5% Open Space Fund dedication from Real Estate Transfer Tax revenue for the 2027 budget year. The argument for: fiscal pressure is real, and a one-year suspension keeps the lights on without permanently touching the program. The argument against: voters backed that land-conservation commitment, and a suspension that keeps recurring starts to look like a policy shift dressed up as a budget fix.

So — is a temporary suspension a reasonable response to a tight year, or does skipping it again cross a line?
choices: Depends on what else gets cut

title: Open space money — or keep the lights on?
body:
Council is voting on a second reading of an ordinance that would suspend the 5% Open Space Fund dedication from Real Estate Transfer Tax revenue for the 2027 budget year. The fund is how the town has long honored a voter expectation around land conservation — skipping a year frees up money when budgets are tight. Supporters say fiscal pressure is real and one year isn't a broken promise. Critics say it sets a pattern and that conservation commitments are easiest to honor when they're inconvenient.

So which is it — a reasonable pause, or the first chip in something that holds?
choices: Depends on what else is cut

title: Should the town rethink how it rents to its own workers?
body:
The Resident Advisory Committee is taking up consulting services for a comprehensive review of Telluride's employee rental housing policies. That means the rules governing who gets town-owned housing, on what terms, could change.

Some residents will say the current policies need a hard look — the workforce has shifted and the housing crunch is real. Others will push back on spending consulting dollars to revisit a system that, however imperfect, is already running.

What do you think — is a full policy review the right move, or not worth the cost?

title: Exception or precedent?
body:
The Telluride Housing Authority Subcommittee has a stack of requests on its plate — residents including Nichole Zangara, Jim Riley, and Anthony and Melannie Tavano are asking for exceptions to the Affordable Housing Guidelines around lenders and mortgages. That's a lot of individual cases at once.

Some will see this as the system working: real people hitting real obstacles, and a process that lets them ask for relief. Others will wonder whether a pile of exception requests signals that the underlying guidelines need a harder look — or whether exceptions, granted often enough, quietly become the new rule.

So: when residents need exceptions to make affordable housing work for them, is that a feature of the system or a sign something's off?
choices: It's the system working as intended
Too many exceptions breaks the rules

title: Old buildings, new changes — who decides what fits?
body:
The Historic and Architectural Review Commission is set to take up applications for Certificates of Appropriateness — meaning proposed changes to structures or signs in Telluride need their sign-off before moving forward. Some residents see that oversight as exactly right: the town's historic character doesn't protect itself. Others find the process slow and subjective — a barrier to owners who want to maintain or improve their own property. Neither complaint is wrong.

Where do you come down — is design review a fair trade for preserving what makes this place worth living in, or does it put too much control in the hands of a commission?
choices: Fair trade for what we have

title: The county wants a housing action plan — but what does that mean?
body:
The Board of County Commissioners is set to consider creating a housing action plan. That sounds straightforward until you ask what it actually commits anyone to. Supporters would say the region's housing crunch demands a real roadmap — something with teeth. Skeptics might wonder whether another plan just means more process, more delay, and outcomes that look good on paper but don't move the needle. Nothing's been adopted yet; this is still at the consideration stage.

So: is a housing action plan a meaningful step forward, or one more document that gathers dust?

title: Who gets to say yes — and who just gets to watch?
body:
The Liquor Licensing Authority is set to review license applications or modifications, but with a catch built into the process: the hearing officer handles most matters, while new licenses require Town Council approval on top of that. So the same question comes up again — how much of this decision really belongs to the licensing body, and how much gets handed up the chain?

Some folks think layered oversight keeps things accountable. Others think it slows things down and muddies who's actually responsible. Where do you land?

title: Hazard plan — worth the county's time right now?
body: The Board of County Commissioners is expected to consider developing a multi-jurisdictional hazard mitigation plan. That means pulling multiple local governments together to map out risks and responses before something goes wrong. Some residents will say that kind of coordinated planning is exactly what a mountain community needs — better late than never. Others may wonder whether it's another layer of process that moves slowly and costs money the county could spend on more immediate needs. Nothing's decided yet. So: is a multi-jurisdictional hazard plan a smart use of county attention right now?

title: New license, new fight — or no fight at all?
body:
The Liquor Licensing Authority meets November 19 to review license applications or modifications. The setup is worth noting: the hearing officer handles most matters, but new licenses require Town Council approval — and both local and state sign-off are needed before anything is issued. Some residents will say that two-step process is exactly the right amount of scrutiny for a small mountain town. Others will say it's a gauntlet that slows legitimate businesses down. Neither side is wrong.

So where do you land — is the dual-approval requirement the right call, or is it more hurdle than help?

title: New pour, new rules
body: The Liquor Licensing Authority meets to act on license applications or modifications. The hearing officer handles most matters, but new licenses require Town Council approval — and both local and state sign-off are needed before anything is issued. That split process is where the tension lives. Some residents see multiple checkpoints as the right way to protect the character of a small town. Others think the layered approval structure slows legitimate business down or gives too many hands a veto. So: does the current approval process strike the right balance — or is it too much gatekeeping for a place this size?

title: Should the town hire a consultant to review its employee housing rules?
body:
Town Council is expected to discuss bringing in consulting services for a comprehensive review of Telluride's employee rental housing policies. That sounds procedural — until you think about what it means.

Some residents will say outside expertise is exactly what's needed: fresh eyes, no local politics, a real audit of whether the rules are working. Others will push back — consultants cost money, and the people who know how employee housing actually functions up here are already in town.

Is outside help the right move for something this local?

title: A trail, a canopy, and a fresh coat for the jail
body:
The Planning Commission has a mixed plate: a connector trail, a fuel island canopy, and painting the county jail are all on the table. Each one sounds routine until you think about what it competes with. Trail access is something a lot of people here care about. Jail upkeep is a public obligation. A fuel canopy is infrastructure. The question is whether these get weighed against each other — or just rubber-stamped one by one.

Which of these would you most want the commission to slow down and scrutinize?

title: Who gets to pour — and who decides?
body:
The Liquor Licensing Authority meets to act on license applications or modifications for local establishments. A hearing officer presides, but new licenses require Town Council approval on top of that — and state sign-off too. Some residents think layered oversight protects the character of a small town. Others figure it slows things down and adds hoops for businesses that already face long odds up here. Both camps have a point.

So where do you land — is multi-level liquor licensing oversight the right call for Telluride, or is it more process than the situation warrants?
choices: State plus town is about right

title: The county wants a housing action plan
body:
The Board of County Commissioners is set to consider creating a housing action plan at its November 18 meeting. No details on what that plan would contain are available yet — it's still a proposal.

That's where the tension lives. Some residents will say a formal plan is long overdue and that without one, housing decisions stay reactive. Others will wonder whether another plan just produces a document that sits on a shelf while the actual problem doesn't move.

So — does a housing action plan change anything, or is the county already past the point where planning helps?

title: Who reviews the rent rules — and does it matter who does it?
body:
Council is moving toward hiring outside consultants to do a comprehensive review of Telluride's employee rental housing policies. Some residents will see that as a smart move — fresh eyes, no local baggage, a real audit of whether the policies are actually working. Others will push back: local housing is a local problem, and paying consultants to study it can feel like a way to delay hard decisions the town already has the information to make. No contract has been approved yet — this is still at the discussion stage.

So where do you land: is outside expertise the right tool here, or is this one the town should work out itself?

title: Should the county have an AI policy — and what should it say?
body: Commissioners are expected to dig into a draft AI resolution and policy, alongside Senate Bill 26-189, at a work session. It's not a final vote — just a conversation. But the tension is real. Some residents will want the county ahead of this, with clear rules before AI tools become routine in government work. Others will wonder why a small mountain county needs a formal AI policy at all, or worry that outside legislation like SB 26-189 is already doing the steering for them. Where do you come down?
choices: Get the policy in place now
Overkill for a county this size
Let the state law handle it

title: One deed restriction, one exception request
body:
The Board of County Commissioners, sitting as the Housing Authority, will consider an exception request from Esperanza Reyes to continuing residency and employment standards under her deed restriction. Deed restrictions on affordable units exist for a reason — they keep housing in local hands over time. But life doesn't always fit the rules: circumstances change, and a flat denial can feel punishing. Some neighbors will say exceptions undermine the whole system. Others will say a case-by-case review is exactly how fair administration works.

Where do you come down — should deed restriction exceptions be granted case by case, or held firm?

title: Gas-powered leaf blowers — next to go?
body: The Ecology Commission is set to review a proposed ordinance that would phase out combustion-powered lawn and garden equipment. Up here, that means gas blowers, trimmers, mowers — the whole category. Supporters will say it's overdue: cleaner air, quieter streets, fewer fumes in a canyon that traps everything. Skeptics will push back on who actually bears the cost — landscapers and contractors switching equipment mid-career aren't absorbing that lightly. Nothing is adopted yet; this is still a review. So: is a phase-out of gas lawn equipment a reasonable next step, or an overreach?

title: Deck repairs — or something more?
body: The Design Review Board has a work session coming up on deck repairs and possible extensions at 120 Vischer Dr. Work sessions are exploratory — nothing's decided yet. But that phrase "possible extensions" is where opinions tend to split. Some neighbors see deck work as routine upkeep that keeps older structures sound. Others worry that a repair conversation quietly becomes an expansion conversation, adding mass or footprint to something that wasn't originally sized for it. Where's the line between fixing what's there and changing what's there?

title: How many boards does it take to hire one consultant?
body: The Planning & Zoning Commission is holding a special meeting to discuss a Request for Proposal for consulting services to review Telluride's employee rental housing policies. It's also on the agenda — in the same week — for the Housing Authority Subcommittee, the Arts & Special Events Commission, Town Council budget talks, and the Ecology Commission. Some residents will see that as thorough, multi-angle vetting before anything changes. Others will wonder why so many boards are weighing in before a consultant is even hired. Who actually drives this process — and does spreading it across this many tables help or slow things down?
choices: Just hire someone and move on

title: One lot line erased on W. Columbia
body:
A minor subdivision application for 510 W Columbia Avenue would vacate the lot line between two existing parcels and merge them into a single roughly 5,625-square-foot lot — Lot 40R. Straightforward on paper. But combining parcels can change what's buildable, and neighbors tend to notice when a lot suddenly has more room to work with. Some will see a reasonable consolidation of property a landowner already holds. Others will wonder what comes next on a freshly enlarged footprint.

What's your read — routine paperwork, or does it matter?

title: A height variance before it's built
body:
The Design Review Board is taking up a height variance request for an undeveloped lot on Mountain Village Blvd. Nothing's approved yet — it's on the agenda, not in the books.

That's where the split usually starts. One side figures variances on empty lots are exactly the right moment to ask: before anything goes up, before neighbors are staring at it. The other side worries that granting height exceptions on undeveloped land sets a precedent that quietly rewrites what the rules actually mean.

So — is a pre-construction variance the responsible time to be flexible, or the riskiest?
choices: Best time to bend the rules

title: Should an outside consultant rewrite the housing rules?
body:
The Telluride Housing Authority Subcommittee is set to discuss a request for proposals to hire outside consulting services for a comprehensive review of the town's employee rental housing policies. That means fresh eyes — but also outside hands — on rules that shape who gets to live up here and under what terms.

Some will see it as overdue: policies calcify, and an independent review could surface fixes insiders are too close to see. Others will wonder whether handing that work to consultants risks losing the local knowledge — and accountability — that should drive housing decisions.

So: is outside expertise the right tool for this, or should the community be leading its own review?

title: Pause the open space fund — or hold the line?
body:
Council is taking up an ordinance that would suspend the 5% capital fund allocation for open space in 2027. It's a first reading, so nothing is decided yet. The argument for: the town is facing budget pressure, and a one-year pause buys room to maneuver. The argument against: open space protection is exactly what gets quietly eroded during tight years, and a suspension sets a precedent. Both sides have a point.

So — is one year off a reasonable trade-off, or does pausing the open space fund open a door that's hard to close?
choices: One year is fine, budgets are tight
Don't touch the open space fund
Sets a bad precedent either way
